doc.title: Pete Levin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Napster, Internet music distribution and record companies
summary: Rowe and Levin discuss downloading, record companies' struggles, and Levin offering a free MP3 track on Amazon.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Well the technology is there so why can’t I use it? And it’s a big temptation. I mean I know I kept telling my own teenage daughters I don’t like this, I don’t think you should be doing it. And then I’ll look on their hard drive and see this song like, “Oh I’d love to have that. Why don’t you burn me a copy of that.” And I go wait a minute now I’m doing it too.

It’s the challenge of course that it’s made the music industry re-think the way they’re distributing music. The record companies, now they’re hurting, they’re feeling it now. They should have dealt with this much earlier. They’re looking for ways to market music over the Internet. And there is no simple answer to it. They just went through a — I don’t know a lot of the details about it — but they spent millions setting up this system of grouping together and selling music over the Internet. They overlooked one small detail, they hadn’t made any deal with the publisher’s associations. And the publisher’s associations said wait a minute, you can’t do that. We own the music, you don’t. So they’re still working on that. But they’ll get there. But the whole system of downloading MP3 files over the Internet — some if it’s done legally, some illegally, but some companies are finding ways to do it in ways that are equitable, which it takes some dealing and it means you’re going to get stolen from sometimes. Like I have a re-issue of a Christmas record that I did ten years ago which now I have out on my own label, and Amazon has it, and I gave them an MP3 of one of the tracks that if you just click on it you can download it. And next to it there’s a thing if you want you can pay a dollar for this or not, it’s a choice of whoever downloads it. And obviously it’s my choice to make it available. And it’s not a sample, it’s the whole track. The objective is simple, if you like this click over there and for fifteen bucks they’ll send you the whole CD. It’s a © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

different concept. You give somebody something and maybe they’ll do it. And that’s just one independent person trying to peddle his own music. Warner Brothers has to do it on a much bigger scale. They have to figure out how to market major artists without getting ripped off so badly that it’s not worth doing it. If it’s costing them two million dollars to produce a CD they can’t afford to get ripped off too badly. So they’ve got to deal with it. It’s a new world. And it started with the Mini Moog which is really something, when the technology was put in the hands of just the guy on the street, the guy in his living room. The Moog synthesizer was huge — I don’t remember what it sold for, it was a lot of money like twenty-five thousand, twenty thousand, that was a lot of money in the 70s. But for two thousand I could carry one in a suitcase, and I did all over Europe. I could do that. The Yamaha — an incredible company — but they came out with a synthesizer, the DX-7 at around 1980, which got lost in the shuffle and it’s a dinosaur now.
